I think DC’s nature spots are underrated. Here’s where to go.

Updated September 1, 2026
Alexandria Taylor
Ask me a question in the comments (0)
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 7:06
Instaread

Washington DC is a bustling city. A beautiful, bustling city with historic neighborhoods, restaurants, and shops. And when you think of a city, you don’t often think of ample green space. 

Of course, there is the National Mall, a large grassy area with many of DC’s famous museums set around it. And most neighborhoods have a park or playground to enjoy the outdoors or for kids to play. However, these places feel like they’re still in the middle of the city… because they are.

If you want a complete nature escape, there are a few places that feel like an oasis where the city is miles away. But surprisingly, they’re in DC or not far from the city. 

As a DC local, these are the nature spots that are underrated and that I think you may want to add to your DC itinerary.

Rock Creek Park

Rock Creek Park is probably DC’s most famous park. With over 1,700 acres in upper Northwest, it’s truly a spot to disappear from the city. When you’re on one of the many hiking, walking, or equestrian trails, it truly feels like you’re in a national park or nature preserve.

There are little to no signs of the city. You hear birds, see wildlife, and can even fish in some areas. While there are a few roads where cars can drive through the park, the majority of them are closed for pedestrians and bikers. The lack of cars contributes to the encompassing nature feeling.

From an after-work run to a leisurely weekend walk, Rock Creek Park is one of the city’s best nature escapes. Find a picnic grove to enjoy an outdoor snack or take a horseback riding lesson. You’ll have plenty of space to enjoy the fresh air, surrounded by old trees, lush plants, and, of course, a babbling creek.

Kenilworth Park and Aquatic Gardens

Kenilworth Park and Gardens is probably one of my favorite nature spots in the city. Though it’s off the highway and tucked into an urban neighborhood, when you come here you won’t feel like you’re in DC at all.

Kenilworth Park and Aquatic Gardens is part of the National Park Service and located in the northeastern part of the city. It’s adjacent to the Anacostia River and is comprised of marshlands and aquatic ecosystems.

What makes this park famous is the lotus and water lily ponds. In the summer, these plants grow tall and bloom with colorful flowers. It really is a sight to see, and it feels like you can get lost between the blooming ponds.

There is also a wooden boardwalk that takes you out over the marshlands. Here you can spot plenty of birds, so it’s a great place if you want to do some birdwatching. While you’re in the gardens, be sure to be on the lookout for turtles, snapping turtles, and even beavers.

Kenilworth is a tranquil spot that’s great for a nature walk or a picnic. Entry is free, so it’s also a great low-cost activity in the city.

👉 Travel Tip: The water lilies and lotuses bloom in July. So if you’re visiting DC in the summer, watch out for an official announcement on peak bloom before you make a trip.

Anacostia River Trail

A 12-mile trail that runs from DC’s Navy Yard neighborhood to Bladenburg, Maryland, the Anacostia River Trail is one of the best places for outdoor activity in DC. On the trail, you can walk, bike, and run along the river. The trail takes you through forested areas, so you’re surrounded by trees in many areas and don’t feel like you’re in the city at all.

My favorite part of the Anacostia River Trail is Bladenburg Waterfront Park in Maryland, which can be the beginning or end of the trail. It’s a river-front park that’s just outside the city and so relaxing.

From Bladenburg Waterfront Park, you can rent kayaks and canoes to boat down the Anacostia. There’s also an entry to the Anacostia River Trail for bikers, walkers, and runners. The park also has a picnic pavilion, fishing pier, and playground.

There are other locations on the Anacostia River Trail to launch kayaks and canoes, and there are also often groups and tours that go down the river. The Anacostia River Trail is one of the best nature places if you’re active or like water sports.

Kingman and Heritage Islands

Kingman and Heritage Islands are man-made islands in DC dedicated to natural resource preservation and education. It’s located right by Anacostia Park in Northeast DC and is a thriving wildlife habitat.

It’s a beautiful place to walk around and do a nature walk; there’s even a self-guided habitat tour where you can learn about the history of the islands and the wildlife that call the islands home.

There are trails through the islands where you can bike, hike, and walk, and even bring your dog along. You can fish on the piers and birdwatch to try to spot one of the one hundred species of resident and migratory birds. Picnic at one of the many tables or explore the waters by boat with kayaks and canoes.

Kingman and Heritage Islands are such a great hidden gem in the city. Go for an evening walk after work or spend a sunny Saturday among nature.

National Arboretum

The National Arboretum is 446 acres and the site of a botanical research center as well as nature grounds in Northeast DC. It’s listed on the National Register of Historic Places, so it’s definitely one of the coolest things to do in DC.

The Arboretum features a variety of major gardens, such as the Asian Collections, the Flowering Tree Collections, and the National Grove of State Trees, all of which feature a beautiful collection of plants. The National Bonsai and Penjing Museum is one of my favorites and seeing such old, well-taken-care-of trees is one of the coolest sights.

The grounds also feature tons of blooming shrubs and trees, including azaleas and magnolias. It’s a colorful and beautiful sight in the spring and summer. Another feature that draws people to the Arboretum is the National Capitol Columns, which are old Corinthian columns that were part of the US Capitol building between 1828 and 1958.

There are walking paths through the Arboretum and places to picnic in the National Grove of State Trees. It’s open daily with extended hours in the summer and admission is free.

***

Living in a city has plenty of benefits, from vibrant neighborhoods, great restaurants and unique museums; and DC is no exception. But sometimes you need a little escape and to be surrounded by nature. 

These nature spots in DC are some of the best places to be surrounded by wildlife, water, and trees without venturing far from DC. These spots are the true definition of an urban oasis.
